claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by rapid thermal annealing can create a hierarchical microstructure consisting of an ultrafine-grained HEA matrix with uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates.
The proposed hierarchical microstructure will increase strength by at least 10–15% relative to conventional processing.
The proposed hierarchical microstructure will increase ductility by at least 10–15% relative to conventional processing.
The proposed hierarchical microstructure will increase fracture resistance by at least 10–15% relative to conventional processing.
The integrated processing route will maintain or modestly enhance Young's modulus.
Conventionally processed HEAs generally have relatively coarse or single-phase microstructures.
Severe plastic deformation refines the HEA grain structure and induces defects.
Rapid thermal annealing after severe plastic deformation can produce a controlled, evenly dispersed nanoscale precipitate population.
The anticipated improvements should occur from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures under quasi-static or dynamic loading.
The method may lose effectiveness at extreme temperatures or very high strain rates because additional failure mechanisms may dominate.
The method may fail in HEAs prone to phase instability when rapid thermal processing cannot control microstructural evolution.
The integrated processing route generates multiscale deformation heterogeneity.
Multiscale deformation heterogeneity activates concurrent dislocation slip and twinning.
The hierarchical microstructure promotes microcrack deflection.
Concurrent slip, twinning, and microcrack deflection produce a better balance of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance.
Traditional HEA processing typically improves one or two mechanical properties at the expense of others.
Analogous hierarchical structures in other alloy systems have produced similar synergistic mechanical-property improvements.
Reproducible and precise control of precipitate distributions in HEAs remains uncertain.
The relationship between in-situ-observed microstructural evolution and macroscopic mechanical performance requires further validation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts simultaneous improvement in strength, ductility, and fracture resistance, but the falsification rule requires improvement in only at least two targeted properties. Thus, failure of one of the three explicitly predicted properties might not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
